column1: A teammate runs usermod -G docker alice intending to add her to the docker group. What goes wrong and what is the safe command?
column2: Bare -G REPLACES the entire supplementary group list with exactly what is specified — alice loses every other group she belonged to (sudo, wheel, etc.), keeping only docker. Safe version: usermod -aG docker alice — -a appends, preserving existing groups. Always verify with id alice before and after.

column1: You add a user to the sudo group on Rocky Linux 9 and sudo still does not work. Why?
column2: sudo is the Debian/Ubuntu group name for sudo access. RHEL-family distros (Rocky, RHEL, CentOS, Amazon Linux, Fedora) use wheel instead. The sudo group likely does not exist or has no sudoers rule on this system. Fix: usermod -aG wheel username. Verify with: grep -E '^%sudo|^%wheel' /etc/sudoers

column1: Why do you always use visudo instead of editing /etc/sudoers directly with a text editor?
column2: visudo validates syntax before saving and refuses to save invalid syntax. A direct text editor save with a syntax error can lock out ALL sudo access on the system, including your own, with no easy recovery if no other root path exists. visudo also works on /etc/sudoers.d/ files via visudo -f /path/to/file.

column1: What is the User Private Group (UPG) scheme? What GID does a new user get by default?
column2: When useradd creates a user with no -g flag, it also creates a new group with the same name and GID as the username, and sets that as the user's primary group. Example: useradd deployer creates both user deployer (UID 1002) and group deployer (GID 1002), with deployer's primary GID = 1002. This means a user's primary group typically matches their username on standard installs.

column1: What makes a service account different from a regular user account? Name two required properties.
column2: Two required properties: (1) Shell set to /usr/sbin/nologin — rejects any interactive login attempt (ssh, su, console) while still allowing systemd to start processes as this user via the unit file's User= directive. (2) No usable password — confirmed via passwd -S showing L (locked) or NP (no password). Typically also created with useradd -r for a system-range UID.

column1: /etc/passwd shows wadmin:x:1000:1000:Wadmin User:/home/wadmin:/bin/bash. What does the x represent and where is the actual password data?
column2: The x is a placeholder meaning 'see /etc/shadow for the password'. /etc/passwd must remain world-readable for many tools to function (e.g. displaying usernames), but storing password hashes in a world-readable file would be a serious vulnerability. /etc/shadow, readable only by root, stores the actual hash plus aging fields (last change, min/max age, warning days, expiry).

column1: chage -l deployer shows 'Account expires: never'. How do you set this account to expire automatically in 30 days, useful for a contractor?
column2: chage -E YYYY-MM-DD deployer — sets a hard account expiry date. After that date, the account becomes unusable automatically without anyone needing to remember to manually disable it. Useful for contractor or temporary access where the end date is known in advance.

column1: What is the difference between a user's primary group and supplementary groups? Which file records each?
column2: Primary group: exactly one per user, recorded in /etc/passwd (the GID field), assigned to new files the user creates by default. Supplementary groups: zero or more, recorded in /etc/group (each group's members field), grant additional access (sudo, wheel, docker, etc.). The kernel checks ALL of a user's groups — primary and supplementary — when evaluating group-based file permissions, not just the primary one.

column1: What is the GECOS field in /etc/passwd, and what does GECOS stand for?
column2: GECOS stands for General Electric Comprehensive Operating System — a 1960s mainframe OS that early Unix systems interfaced with, requiring a contact/account field in /etc/passwd. On modern Linux it is simply a free-text comment field, typically used for a user's full name or a service account's purpose description. Format: comma-delimited (Full name, Room, Work phone, Home phone, Other) — most systems only fill the first subfield. Change with usermod -c or chfn.

column1: What does $y$ mean at the start of a hash in /etc/shadow? What about $6$?
column2: $y$ = yescrypt — the DEFAULT on Ubuntu 22.04 and later (including 24.04). $6$ = SHA-512 — the default on Rocky/RHEL 8+ and Ubuntu 14.04-20.04. Check your system with: grep ENCRYPT_METHOD /etc/login.defs. Yescrypt is deliberately slow and memory-intensive, making GPU brute-force attacks orders of magnitude more expensive than SHA-512.

column1: What is the difference between su and sudo? When should each be used?
column2: su (substitute user) opens a full shell as another user for the duration of the session and requires the TARGET user's password. sudo (superuser do) runs ONE command with elevated privileges using YOUR OWN password, governed by /etc/sudoers rules, and logs every command with username+timestamp. Modern practice: use sudo for interactive admin tasks (sudo -i replaces su -), never distribute root passwords, revoke access per-user by removing from sudoers/wheel group.

column1: A syntax error on one line of /etc/sudoers — does it break just that rule or the entire file?
column2: The entire file. sudo parses the whole file before every command. If it finds ANY syntax error anywhere, it refuses to honour ANY rule in the entire file — including rules for other users that are syntactically correct. Result: all sudo access is removed system-wide until the syntax is fixed. This is why visudo is mandatory — it validates syntax before saving and refuses to write an invalid file.

column1: What is the difference between password inactive, password expiry, and account expiry in /etc/shadow?
column2: Password expiry (maxage): forces a password CHANGE at next login — doesn't lock you out, just demands a new password. Password inactive: grace period AFTER password expires — if the user doesn't log in during this window, the account locks entirely (no more 'change your password' prompt). Account expiry (chage -E): hard date when the ACCOUNT becomes completely unusable regardless of password state — no authentication method works. Three independent lockout mechanisms.
